context_blurb:
Split open the right rock, and you might find a shell, a leaf or a fish bone from long, long ago. Many rocks are built in layers, laid down one after another like the pages of a book. Those layers hold fossils, and fossils are clues to what the land was like long ago.

A muddy river carries sand, mud, crumbs of rock and broken shells. When it flows into a calm lake or sea, it slows down, and the bits sink to the bottom. Bits like these, carried along by water, wind or ice and dropped somewhere else, are called sediment. Year after year, new sediment settles on top of the old, so it builds up in layers.

Given thousands to millions of years, buried sediment hardens into rock. The weight of the upper layers presses down on the lower ones, squeezing the grains tightly together and pushing out the water between them. Minerals in that water then stick the grains to one another, the way cement holds a sidewalk together. So the grains are pressed together and glued by minerals: sand becomes sandstone, and mud becomes shale, a rock that splits into thin, flat sheets. Mud that only dries in the Sun has not become rock. Rock made in layers this way is called sedimentary rock.

Some rock is made from living things. In warm, shallow seas, the shells of sea creatures and bits of coral heap up on the bottom, and over ages the heap hardens into limestone. Limestone is made mostly of calcium carbonate, the hard stuff of shells and corals, so it is often packed with fossil shells.

A fossil is any remains, print or trace of a living thing from long ago, usually more than ten thousand years old. Bones, teeth and shells are fossils, and so are footprints, burrows and the prints of leaves. When a fern leaf falls in soft mud and rots away, its outline can stay pressed in the rock that the mud becomes. That print counts as a fossil, because a living thing left it. A shape in a rock that no living thing made is not a fossil.

Few living things ever become fossils. A body left out in the open is eaten by scavengers or rots away. A dead fish has its best chance when mud and sand bury it quickly. The cover keeps scavengers off and slows rotting, so the hard bones last long enough to be saved.

That is why most fossils are found in sedimentary rock, built from layers of sand and mud: the layers bury remains gently, without great heat. Rock that forms from melted rock, such as cooled lava, almost never holds a fossil, because the melted rock wipes the remains away.

Now and then a tiny creature is saved whole. Amber began as resin, a thick, sticky liquid that oozes from some trees. An insect that landed in fresh resin stuck fast and was sealed in, and over millions of years the buried resin hardened into amber, often clear and golden, with the insect still inside. Many books call the resin sap.

Fossils show how places have changed. Corals and starfish live only in the sea, never in lakes or rivers. So a rock layer full of their fossils under a dry field shows that an ocean once covered the land.

Buried life can even become fuel. Most oil formed from trillions of tiny living things, algae and plankton, that drifted in ancient seas, then died, sank to the sea floor and were buried in mud. Deep underground, heat and pressure slowly changed them into oil, and natural gas often formed alongside. Oil does not come from dinosaurs; that is a myth. Coal formed mostly from the plants of ancient swamps. Because coal, oil and natural gas all formed from the buried remains of living things, they are called fossil fuels.
